title: Dabrafenib and trametinib for advanced BRAF-mutated melanoma
context_label: NCCP 00415a: unresectable or metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation. This route covers advanced disease; the separate 00415/adjuvant guide covers the 12-month postoperative setting.
purpose: Dabrafenib and trametinib block two points in a growth pathway used by BRAF V600-mutated melanoma. In this advanced-disease setting the aim is disease control, with the effect on symptoms, side effects and your priorities reviewed regularly.
schedule_summary: Take dabrafenib twice daily, around 12 hours apart, and trametinib once daily. Both are taken every day unless the team instructs a hold. safety_note: The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

consent_support: Discuss the exact diagnosis, treatment intent, expected benefits and uncertainty, suitable alternatives, the regimen-specific risks and monitoring, fertility and pregnancy precautions, and practical burdens. Confirm the treatment phase and route. This guide supports the conversation and does not replace individual consent.
urgent_extra: Fever is a particular concern. At 38°C or above, withhold both medicines and contact the oncology team promptly under the written fever plan; recurrent episodes may require action at the first symptoms. Infection and dehydration also need assessment. Restart only when the team tells you. Urgent help is also needed for vision change, severe rash, chest pain, breathlessness, bleeding or severe muscle symptoms.

agents.name: Dabrafenib
agents.explanation: Dabrafenib inhibits an altered BRAF protein that sends growth signals inside eligible melanoma cells. Trametinib blocks another step in that pathway. The tumour’s BRAF result is checked before selecting this treatment.
agents.watch: Fever needs the written hold/contact plan. Check other medicines and contraception because interactions can matter.
risks: Skin rash and new skin tumours
Harm to pregnancy and drug interactions

agents.name: Trametinib
agents.explanation: Trametinib inhibits MEK proteins, which pass growth signals onward inside cells. It is used with dabrafenib in this plan. Normal tissues can also be affected, so heart checks and prompt reporting of eye or breathing symptoms remain important.
agents.watch: Attend cardiac tests. New eye symptoms, cough, breathlessness, swelling or severe diarrhoea need prompt review.
risks: Bleeding, liver changes and muscle injury

passport_visit_note: Record the actual date, treatment received, any hold, important symptom and the next check. A review visit is not automatically a medicine dose or a completed cycle.
anatomy_note: The established anatomical illustration links body areas to the full regimen-specific descriptions. A body location helps explain possible effects; it does not diagnose the cause of a symptom or indicate its frequency.
anatomy: At 38°C or above, hold both medicines and contact the team under your fever plan. Infection and dehydration must also be considered.
Report blurred vision, eye pain, redness, light sensitivity or a change in sight promptly; some eye problems need urgent specialist treatment.
Keep ECG and heart ultrasound checks. New breathlessness, swollen ankles, palpitations or chest pain needs prompt assessment.
Rash and skin sensitivity may occur; new changing spots need review. Blistering, peeling or mouth sores with a rash needs urgent help.
Liver changes may first appear in blood tests. Report yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, unusual itching or upper-abdominal pain.
Fever, vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and kidney problems. Call for reduced urine, dizziness or inability to keep fluids down.
Aches can occur. Severe muscle pain or weakness, especially with dark urine, needs urgent advice and possible blood tests.
Tell the team about persistent diarrhoea, vomiting or pain. Severe abdominal pain, blood or black stools needs urgent assessment.

chronology_notes.text: The missed-dose windows differ: take missed dabrafenib only when more than six hours remain before the next dose; take missed trametinib only when more than 12 hours remain. support.title: Fever action plan
support.text: If temperature reaches 38°C or higher, withhold both dabrafenib and trametinib and contact your oncology team promptly for assessment. For recurrent episodes, the team may advise withholding at the first symptom. Restarting needs the team’s plan after at least 24 hours without symptoms; do not use this as an automatic self-restart rule.

support.title: An individual symptom plan
support.text: Ask which anti-sickness or other symptom medicines are prescribed, when to take them and when to call if they do not help. Do not start a borrowed medicine or alter treatment to manage a side effect yourself.

support.title: Your urgent contacts
support.text: Keep your actual oncology, out-of-hours and pharmacy contacts on the wallet card. Example numbers on a template must be replaced before you use it.

support.title: Pregnancy and fertility precautions
support.text: Discuss fertility and pregnancy precautions before starting. Use an effective alternative to hormonal contraception during treatment and for two weeks after dabrafenib and 16 weeks after trametinib; dabrafenib can make hormonal contraception less effective. The team must confirm the method and the later applicable end date for the combination. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask when it is safe to resume. Report a possible pregnancy promptly.

support.title: Eating, activity and practical help
support.text: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use these questions with your own pathology report and agreed treatment plan.

items.title: What the diagnosis says
items.text: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

items.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
items.text: A BRAF V600 result identifies whether the targeted medicines in this plan can act on the tumour. Keep the laboratory result and date. A tumour change is not, on its own, evidence of an inherited condition.

items.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
items.text: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

items.title: Stage and response are different
items.text: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

items.title: A new skin change still needs review
items.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

chapters.title: Your medicines and the overall plan
chapters.intro: Dabrafenib and trametinib block two points in a growth pathway used by BRAF V600-mutated melanoma. In this advanced-disease setting the aim is disease control, with the effect on symptoms, side effects and your priorities reviewed regularly.

items.title: The schedule in this setting
items.text: Take dabrafenib twice daily, around 12 hours apart, and trametinib once daily. Both are taken every day unless the team instructs a hold. Treatment for advanced melanoma continues while beneficial and tolerable; there is no preset cycle total. A 28-day calendar is a review period, not a treatment-free week.

items.title: How the treatment works
items.text: A BRAF V600 change can keep the cell-growth pathway switched on. Dabrafenib blocks the altered BRAF protein. It is paired with a MEK inhibitor to act on the same pathway at another point. The BRAF result comes from tumour testing; it does not automatically mean a hereditary condition. MEK carries growth signals further along the pathway below BRAF. Trametinib blocks MEK alongside dabrafenib. Normal heart, eye, lung and other tissues can also be affected, which is why scheduled tests and prompt symptom reporting matter.

items.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
items.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

items.title: Pauses and stopping
items.text: A safety pause is an active treatment decision. Record which medicine is paused, the reason, the tests or recovery needed and who may authorise restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription or reset the history when a new phase begins.

chapters.title: Taking treatment and preparing for visits
chapters.intro: Keep the written medicine plan beside this guide; it records your own dose and dates.

items.title: Taking or receiving the medicine
items.text: Swallow the prescribed capsules/tablet whole with water. Take each dose at least one hour before food or at least two hours after food. Take the once-daily trametinib dose at the same time each day, alongside either the morning or evening dabrafenib dose according to your written plan. Keep the prescribed storage instructions.

items.title: Missed, vomited or held treatment
items.text: The missed-dose windows differ: take missed dabrafenib only when more than six hours remain before the next dose; take missed trametinib only when more than 12 hours remain. Otherwise skip it. Do not double up. Do not take an extra trametinib dose after vomiting; contact the team or pharmacist about any vomited or uncertain dose.

items.title: Other medicines and supplements
items.text: Show the pharmacist a current list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products and supplements. Include anticoagulants, heart medicines, steroids and recent antibiotics. Check before adding, stopping or changing anything; an apparently harmless product can alter treatment or confuse a symptom assessment.

items.title: Practical preparation
items.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

chapters.title: Tests: what is required and what each result means
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and response scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Confirm the BRAF V600 tumour result and advanced-disease treatment goal. Full blood count, kidney/liver tests, ECG and echocardiogram, skin examination and eye assessment when indicated.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver tests monthly. ECG and echocardiogram at four weeks, then every 12 weeks and after dose modification. Regular skin reviews are required; your oncology team will confirm and record the interval. Head/neck examination every three months and chest CT every six months are specified surveillance checks; disease-response imaging follows the individual plan.

items.title: Scans and tumour markers
items.text: Ask the team to write the next assessment and who will arrange it. Bloods used to monitor kidneys, liver, hormones or muscle are not automatically measures of cancer response. There is no universal tumour-marker blood schedule for these skin-cancer regimens; a scan or extra blood test is requested for a specific clinical reason.

items.title: After a pause or finish
items.text: Continue skin surveillance for six months after stopping as specified by the regimen, and arrange the ongoing melanoma follow-up plan. Review symptoms, heart/eye concerns and contraception instructions after treatment.

items.title: Getting the result
items.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: You can feel well and still need the planned checks. New symptoms deserve attention even on a day without an appointment.

items.title: Your usual pattern
items.text: Record the start and change in symptoms, temperature if advised, bowel pattern, drinking, urine and the effect on normal tasks. A simple few-line record is enough. Use it to describe a change rather than trying to grade or diagnose a toxicity yourself.

items.title: When to call
items.text: Fever is a particular concern. At 38°C or above, withhold both medicines and contact the oncology team promptly under the written fever plan; recurrent episodes may require action at the first symptoms. Infection and dehydration also need assessment. Restart only when the team tells you. Urgent help is also needed for vision change, severe rash, chest pain, breathlessness, bleeding or severe muscle symptoms.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

items.title: A held dose and a new phase
items.text: The missed-dose windows differ: take missed dabrafenib only when more than six hours remain before the next dose; take missed trametinib only when more than 12 hours remain. Otherwise skip it. Do not double up. Do not take an extra trametinib dose after vomiting; contact the team or pharmacist about any vomited or uncertain dose.

chapters.title: Skin checks, sun protection and optional photographs
chapters.intro: This complements clinical assessment and does not replace it.

items.title: Protect your skin
items.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

items.title: Know the pattern of your skin
items.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

items.title: Photographs are optional
items.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

items.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
items.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

chapters.title: Pregnancy, fertility and protecting others
chapters.intro: Discuss these precautions before treatment even if pregnancy is not currently planned.

items.title: Medicine-specific precautions
items.text: Discuss fertility and pregnancy precautions before starting. Use an effective alternative to hormonal contraception during treatment and for two weeks after dabrafenib and 16 weeks after trametinib; dabrafenib can make hormonal contraception less effective. The team must confirm the method and the later applicable end date for the combination. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask when it is safe to resume. Report a possible pregnancy promptly.

items.title: Planning ahead
items.text: Ask early about fertility preservation, sexual health and symptoms affecting intimacy. Tell the team about any chance of pregnancy, breastfeeding or a partner’s pregnancy so that the correct medicine-specific advice can be given. Keep the precautions and their end dates in the written plan.

items.title: Safe handling and supply
items.text: Do not share anticancer medicines. Keep oral medicines in their original labelled packaging, away from children and anyone who could take them accidentally. Return unused medicines to the supplying pharmacy and follow its handling advice. A treatment hold does not remove pregnancy precautions.

chapters.title: Questions, decisions and practical support
chapters.intro: Your priorities and the burden of treatment belong in the discussion.

items.title: Benefits and uncertainties
items.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

items.title: Alternatives and review points
items.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

items.title: Help with daily life
items.text: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.

items.title: Shared understanding
items.text: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.

chapters.title: Follow-up and your continuing record
chapters.intro: Keep this record when treatment is paused, changed or completed.

items.title: Your follow-up plan
items.text: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.

items.title: Continuing medicine precautions
items.text: Continue skin surveillance for six months after stopping as specified by the regimen, and arrange the ongoing melanoma follow-up plan. Review symptoms, heart/eye concerns and contraception instructions after treatment.

items.title: Treatment summary for other clinicians
items.text: Record the medicines and last dates, important reactions, any long-term hormone replacement or steroid taper, and the responsible oncology contact. Show this information in urgent care and to other specialists. A different treatment phase does not erase earlier toxicity.

items.title: The complete paper version
items.text: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Dabrafenib and trametinib block two points in a growth pathway used by BRAF V600-mutated melanoma. In this advanced-disease setting the aim is disease control, with the effect on symptoms, side effects and your priorities reviewed regularly.

questions.q: Is there a fixed number of cycles?
questions.a: Take dabrafenib twice daily, around 12 hours apart, and trametinib once daily. Both are taken every day unless the team instructs a hold. Treatment for advanced melanoma continues while beneficial and tolerable; there is no preset cycle total. A 28-day calendar is a review period, not a treatment-free week.

questions.q: What happens if treatment is held?
questions.a: The missed-dose windows differ: take missed dabrafenib only when more than six hours remain before the next dose; take missed trametinib only when more than 12 hours remain. Otherwise skip it. Do not double up. Do not take an extra trametinib dose after vomiting; contact the team or pharmacist about any vomited or uncertain dose.

Blood count, kidney/liver tests monthly. ECG and echocardiogram at four weeks, then every 12 weeks and after dose modification. Regular skin reviews are required: ask the team to document the interval because the source gives monthly and 60-day instructions in different sections. Head/neck examination every three months and chest CT every six months are specified surveillance checks; disease-response imaging follows the individual plan. Your team adds the actual dates.

questions.q: Can I use this without a smartphone?
questions.a: Yes. The full handbook, three-page summary and wallet card are printable. The QR code is optional; keep actual contacts and written appointments on the paper copy.
